title: Key squares and opposition
summary: Know when king and pawn beat the lone king, and bring your king to the key squares before touching the pawn.
part.keySquares.title: Key squares
part.keySquares.summary: The squares that, once the king stands on one, make sure the pawn queens, whoever is to move.
part.opposition.title: The opposition
part.opposition.summary: With the kings face to face, one square between them and the other side to move, your king climbs from key square to key square up to the sixth rank.
ex.e09: Gligorić against {{Fischer|bobby-fischer}}, 1959. Only one move holds.
ex.e09.hint: If your king steps forward now, the white king gets the opposition. Choose a square from which you can stand face to face with it, whichever square it comes up to.
ex.e09.solution: 57...Kb8! Only then, when the white king comes up, Black takes the opposition: 58.Kc5 Kc7 or 58.Kb5 Kb7. That is what {{Fischer|bobby-fischer}} played, and the white king never reached the key squares a6, b6 and c6.
ex.e10: A position by Jan Drtina, 1908. The direct road does not work.
ex.e10.hint: The key squares are b5, c5 and d5. Through the centre the black king gets there first; try the other side of the pawn.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Kc2!, then 2.Kb3 and 3.Kb4. After 3...Kc6, 4.Kc4 takes the direct opposition, Black has to give way with 4...Kd6 and the white king enters b5. If the white king went down the d-file, the black king would reach c6, take the opposition and draw.
ex.e12: Play White and find the best move. The kings are on the same file, and the pawn stands beside your king.
ex.e12.hint: The key squares of the d4-pawn are c6, d6 and e6. If the kings face each other, with one square between them and Black to move, the black king is the one that gives way: think how to reach that situation.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Ke5! takes the direct opposition: the kings face each other, with e6 between them, and the black king has to give way, whatever move it makes. After 1...Kd8, 2.Kd6 (2.Ke6 also wins) takes the king to a key square, and the pawn queens. 1.d5? and 1.Kd5? only draw: after 1.d5? Kd6 the black king stands in front of the pawn, and after 1.Kd5? Kd7 Black takes the opposition.
ex.e14: Maróczy against {{Marshall|frank-marshall}}, {{Monte Carlo|monte-carlo}} 1903. You play Black, and the pawn is yours; the white king waits on g2.
ex.e14.hint: The key squares of the g5-pawn are f3, g3 and h3, and the white king watches them from g2. The pawn waits: think which square brings your king closer to them.
ex.e14.solution: 58...Kg4! The king goes in front of the pawn, towards the key squares; 58...g4? and 58...Kh5? only draw. After 59.Kh2, 59...Kf3: the black king reaches a key square, and the win is certain, whatever the defence. 59...Kf4 and 59...Kh4 also win.
ex.e15: The pawns are blocked, and your king is further away than Black's. Find the winning move.
ex.e15.hint: A blocked pawn has key squares too. For your king they are the squares on the sixth rank beside the b6-pawn: a6, c6, d6 and e6. For the black king, the ones on the fifth: a5, c5, d5 and e5. Whoever gets there first wins, and the shortest road is the diagonal.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kg3! and the king walks down the diagonal: 2.Kf4, 3.Ke5, 4.Kd5 and, after 4...Kc7, 5.Ke6 (5.Ke5 also works). With the king on a key square, it goes through d7 and c7 and wins the b6-pawn. 1.Kg3, 2.Kf4, 3.Ke5 and 4.Kd5 are all only moves: 1.Kg2? or 1.Kg1? waste a tempo and draw; 1.Kh3? and 1.Kh1? arrive late and even lose, because the black king reaches c5 or d5 first. The example comes from {{Jesús de la Villa|jesus-de-la-villa}}'s book.
ex.e16: Both kings are one step from the enemy pawn. Only one move does not lose. Find the winning move.
ex.e16.hint: It is mutual zugzwang: whoever has to move once the kings face the pawns loses his own. Attack e6 from a square that still leaves you a spare square for the next move.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kd7! The king already eyes e6 and keeps d6 as a spare square. After 1...Kf5, 2.Kd6! Now Black is in zugzwang, and the black king has to leave f5; after 2...Kg6, 3.Kxe6 (3.Ke7 also wins). 1.Kd6?? straight away loses: 1...Kf5 and the zugzwang changes sides. Every other move loses too. {{Jesús de la Villa|jesus-de-la-villa}}'s example.
key.count: A pawn that has not yet passed the fourth rank has three key squares, two ranks in front of it: the square on the same file and its two neighbours. If the white king reaches one of them, the pawn queens, whoever is to move.
key.averbakh: The white king is already on a key square, in front of the pawn. Now it moves forward using the opposition, always ahead of the pawn, up to the sixth rank: White wins.
key.opposition: A trap: taking the opposition out of habit only draws here. What wins is the white king stepping forward, beside the pawn, towards the key squares. The opposition is a means, not an end.
history: King and pawn against king is the most basic ending in chess, and it turns up at the end of many games: knowing whether it wins or draws tells you whether to trade everything off beforehand. It looks simple, but one wrong king step turns a win into a draw, and it has happened to champions. The great shortcut comes from the Russian {{Yuri Averbakh|yuri-averbakh}}: instead of calculating, look for the key squares, the squares that guarantee the win once your king steps on them. He compared the king to a father crossing the street ahead of his child. In 1959, at the {{Candidates|candidates}} Tournament, the young {{Fischer|bobby-fischer}} saved half a point against Gligorić by finding the only king route that held the draw. And in 2009, playing blindfold, {{Kramnik|vladimir-kramnik}} drew against {{Kamsky|gata-kamsky}} by keeping his king firmly in front of the pawn.
practice: Now the real ending: king on d2, pawn on g2, and the black king waiting. Count the key squares, lead with the king and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
part.diagonal.title: Diagonal opposition
part.diagonal.summary: If going straight ahead hands the opposition to the other king, come in on the diagonal with one square between the kings; on the reply, stand face to face and he gives way.
key.diagonal: The opposition works along the diagonal too: the white king stands on the same diagonal as the black king and, step by step, turns it into face-to-face opposition.
ex.e20: Play White and find the best move. The kings are on different files, and the black king watches the pawn's path.
ex.e20.hint: The pawn's key squares are e4, f4 and g4. Your king does not need to go to the black king's file: the opposition also works on a diagonal.
ex.e20.solution: 1.Kd5! The kings stand on a diagonal, with e6 between them, and Black to move: the diagonal opposition is yours. After 1...Kf6, 2.Ke4! The white king reaches e4, a key square, and the pawn will promote. Any other first move lets the black king get there first and draws; pushing the pawn, with 1.f3? or 1.f4?, too, because the pawn goes ahead of the king.
ex.e20.r1: 1...Kf6. The black king approaches the pawn and wants to close your king's path to e4, f4 and g4.
ex.e22: Play Black and find the best move. The white king is closer to the pawn, but has not reached the key squares yet.
ex.e22.hint: The key squares of the b2-pawn are a4, b4 and c4, and the white king already threatens one of them. Your king must arrive in time to shut them all.
ex.e22.solution: 1...Kb5! Only from this square does the black king watch a4, b4 and c4 at once. After 2.Kd3, 2...Kb4! The black king stands on a key square, in front of the pawn, and the white king has no way through: it is a draw. 1...Ka5? does not watch c4 or c5: after 2.Kc5, the white king gets ahead of the pawn and White wins.
